description_full: Copa Holdings, S.A., through its subsidiaries, provides airline passenger, and cargo and mail transportation services in North America, South America, Central America, and the Caribbean. As of December 31, 2025, it operated through a fleet of 125 aircraft. The company was founded in 1947 and is based in Panama City, Panama.
ceo_bio: Mr. Pedro  Heilbron | CEO & Executive Chairman | Age 67
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 8K people. Revenue per employee of $422K ranks in the above the sector median among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $39K of free cash flow annually.
financial_summary: Copa Holdings, S.A. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $5.8B market cap on $3.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 8% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $335M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.71× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 45× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 23% operating margin runs 14pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.06x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 16% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market.
About $36.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 75% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 57% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 29% below its DCF fair value of $202, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $139 to $295 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 9.4 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 6.4 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 17.4 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 11% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 5.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $179 on average, 25% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.19).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.71x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 15pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($387.6M of cash against $1.8B of debt), with interest covered 45.2x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.9% over 3 years and 35.2% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 50%).
At current returns, reinvesting 91% of profits supports about 17.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Analysts expect 26.9% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 93%.
It returns 4.6% a year to shareholders (4.8% in dividends).
people: With about 8,565 employees, each generates about $422K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.6% a year.
That works out to $39K of free cash flow per employee.
